questions.q: What is the role of the crumple zones at the front and rear of the car?
options: To improve normal braking
To strengthen the car so it does not deform at all
To reduce manufacturing cost
To absorb impact energy in a crash and protect the passenger cell
questions.explain: Crumple zones are designed to fold and absorb impact energy, so that the passenger cell around the people stays rigid and protected.

questions.q: What does the seatbelt pretensioner do at the moment of a crash?
options: It tightens the belt instantly to shorten how far the body moves forward
It applies the brakes automatically
It inflates an airbag instead of the belt
It loosens the belt to make it more comfortable
questions.explain: The pretensioner tightens the belt within a fraction of a second, to reduce the distance the body travels forward before it stops.

questions.q: Why are airbags designed to work together with the seatbelt, rather than instead of it?
options: Because airbags are too expensive to operate on their own
Because the law bans deploying an airbag without a fastened seatbelt
Because someone who is not belted can be injured by the airbag itself, reaching it at the wrong speed and angle
Because the airbag only inflates if the seatbelt is fastened
questions.explain: The airbag is designed to catch a body that has already been partly slowed by the seatbelt. Without a belt, the body reaches it at too high a speed.

questions.q: What is the role of a correctly adjusted head restraint?
options: To improve rear visibility
Comfort only, with no effect on safety
To replace the seatbelt in a minor crash
To prevent neck injury ("whiplash") in a rear-end collision
questions.explain: A head restraint at the right height and distance stops the head from snapping backwards forcefully in a rear-end collision, reducing neck injury.

questions.q: Where must a rear-facing child seat never be placed?
options: In a front seat with an active airbag there
In any seat with a three-point seatbelt
In the rear right seat
In the rear middle seat
questions.explain: A front airbag inflating can badly injure a baby sitting in a rear-facing seat.

questions.q: When does the ESC light flash on the instrument cluster?
options: When the engine overheats
When you need to refuel
When the system is switched off
When the system is actually acting to stabilise the car
questions.explain: The ESC light flashes at exactly the moment the system intervenes to stabilise the car; it stays lit steadily when it is switched off or faulty.

questions.q: What does stability control (ESC) do when it detects that the car is drifting from the direction the steering wheel is asking for?
options: It switches off the engine
It brakes a single wheel, and sometimes cuts engine power, to turn the car back towards the intended direction
It increases the car's speed to stabilise it
It inflates an airbag
questions.explain: ESC brakes a single wheel in a targeted way, and sometimes also cuts engine power, to bring the car back to the intended direction of travel.

questions.q: What does traction control (TCS) do when a driven wheel spins during acceleration?
options: It increases engine power to pull away faster
It switches off the steering system
It cuts engine power or brakes the spinning wheel, to transfer drive to a wheel with grip
It has no effect on wheel spin
questions.explain: TCS cuts engine power or brakes the spinning wheel, and transfers the drive to a wheel that has grip.

questions.q: What can ESC not do?
options: Create grip between the tyre and the road that is not there
Act automatically without the driver's involvement
Brake a single wheel
Detect a deviation from the intended direction of travel
questions.explain: ESC makes better use of the grip that exists, but it cannot increase the friction between the tyre and the road.

questions.q: When is it justified to switch off stability control with its dedicated switch?
options: In special situations like deep sand or mud
On every drive in the rain
Never — the switch is just decorative
In ordinary urban road driving
questions.explain: Switching off stability control is meant for special situations like deep sand or mud, where the intervention actually gets in the way — not for ordinary driving.

questions.q: What does AEB do?
options: It warns of a vehicle in the blind spot
It keeps a constant distance from the vehicle ahead only
It reads speed signs
It brakes the car automatically if it detects a hazard and the driver has not reacted in time
questions.explain: AEB (autonomous emergency braking) brakes the car automatically to prevent or reduce a crash the driver has not reacted to in time.

questions.q: What is the difference between LDW and LKA?
options: LDW only warns of lane drift; LKA also gently corrects the steering
Both only work while parking
LDW corrects the steering; LKA only warns
There is no difference, they are the same abbreviation
questions.explain: LDW only warns with a sound or vibration; LKA goes a step further and gently corrects the steering to bring the car back into its lane.

questions.q: What is adaptive cruise control (ACC) used for?
options: Detecting driver fatigue
Warning of lane drift only
Parking the car automatically
Holding a constant speed and slowing down automatically to keep a gap from the vehicle ahead
questions.explain: ACC combines holding a constant speed with automatic slowing and accelerating to keep a gap from the vehicle ahead.

questions.q: What can make traffic sign recognition miss a sign or misread it?
options: Driving at low speed
Running the air conditioning
A dirty, hidden or old sign
Driving on an urban road
questions.explain: Traffic sign recognition relies on a camera, and a dirty, hidden or old sign makes it hard for it to read correctly.

questions.q: What is true about ADAS systems?
options: They replace the need to check mirrors and signal
They amount to full autonomous driving
They are assistance only, and do not replace attention and checking the mirrors
They are only meant for electric vehicles
questions.explain: Assistance systems complement each other, but none of them replaces attention, checking the mirrors and signalling in time.

questions.q: What harms the performance of the cameras and radar in assistance systems?
options: Low speed
Driving on a sunny day
Driving on a straight road
Rain, fog, dirt and ice
questions.explain: Exactly like the driver's eyes, cameras and radar lose accuracy in rain, fog, glare, and dirt or ice on the sensor.

questions.q: Why won't active lane keeping work well on a road with faded lane markings?
options: The system uses only GPS
The system detects the lane from a line marked on the road, and without a clear line it has nothing to align to
Faded lane markings improve detection
The system is not affected by lane markings at all
questions.explain: Lane keeping relies on visually detecting the lane lines; without a clear marking, the system has nothing to align to.

questions.q: What is the greatest risk in driver-assistance systems?
options: They only work at night
The driver's over-reliance, stopping paying attention because they trust the system to catch every mistake
Their high price
They always cause a crash
questions.explain: The main danger is not a system fault but a drop in the driver's alertness, wrongly assuming the system will correct every mistake.

questions.q: Who holds legal responsibility for safe driving in a car with advanced assistance systems?
options: The car manufacturer alone
The insurance company
The driver, always
The system itself
questions.explain: Israeli law does not recognise "autonomous" driving that releases the driver from responsibility — it always stays with the driver.

questions.q: What is true about a pedestrian who suddenly steps out from between two parked cars?
options: This situation does not actually occur in Israel
Assistance systems will always detect them in time
The systems only detect vehicles, never pedestrians, under any circumstances
They may not always be detected in time by assistance systems, just as a driver might miss them
questions.explain: Unusual obstacles that appear suddenly may not be detected in time, even by advanced assistance systems.
